items.explanation: Smith's map was a product of the Virginia Company era: joint-stock companies needed to attract investors and settlers, and maps advertising the Chesapeake's rivers, villages, and resources served that promotional purpose — even as the colony itself was struggling through the starving time.
items.fact_source: u2.md §The story — Jamestown began badly with the starving time of 1609-1610; the Virginia Company learned to pay people to come; §Key terms (Joint-stock company)

option_explanations.A: Wrong because this map charted the Chesapeake for colonization, not a naval search for the Northwest Passage.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the Spanish made their own maps; Smith mapped for English readers and investors.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because Smith was a Chesapeake colonist, not a New England Puritan missionary.
option_explanations.D: Right because company-sponsored maps promoted American ventures to the investors and migrants the colony needed.

options: (A) The Royal Navy's search for a Northwest Passage to Asia through the North American interior
(B) Spanish efforts to locate and destroy English settlements along the Atlantic coast
(C) Puritan missionaries' need for inland routes to reach distant Native villages
(D) Joint-stock companies' need to attract investors and settlers to American ventures
items.stem: This 1612 map by John Smith charted the Chesapeake region for English readers. Which broader development best explains the context in which maps like this were produced?

items.explanation: New Amsterdam was the capital of a Dutch commercial empire built on trade. England seized New Netherland in 1664 precisely to absorb that commerce, and the colony's Dutch legacy — along with Penn's 'holy experiment' — made the Middle Colonies diverse from the start.
items.fact_source: u2.md §The story — the Middle Colonies were diverse from the start: Dutch New Netherland (seized by England in 1664) became New York

option_explanations.A: Right because the settlement's commercial value is what drew both Dutch investment and English seizure.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because New Amsterdam had no gold mines; its wealth was in trade.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the Dutch colony was commercial, not a mission system.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the Armada was defeated in 1588, decades before this settlement's importance, and not by Dutch colonial shipyards.

options: (A) Its role as a commercial hub, seized by England in 1664 to absorb Dutch commerce
(B) Its gold mines, which financed the Dutch war of independence
(C) Its mission system, which converted thousands of Native peoples
(D) Its shipyards, which built the vessels that defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588
items.stem: This 1660 plan shows New Amsterdam, the Dutch colonial capital. Which broader development best explains the context of Dutch and then English interest in this settlement?

items.explanation: The claim is about how England conceived of the colonies, and the strongest support is the doctrine behind the laws. Mercantilism held that colonies existed to enrich the mother country through a favorable balance of trade — the Navigation Acts were that doctrine applied to shipping and ports.
items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms (Mercantilism) — colonies existed to enrich the mother country through a favorable balance of trade; (Navigation Acts) — requiring colonial trade to use English ships and pass through English ports

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the Acts restricted colonial trade; they did not grant assemblies tariff powers.
option_explanations.B: Right because mercantilist doctrine is the direct evidence that England viewed colonies as managed economic assets.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the Acts persisted for over a century; they were not quickly repealed.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the Acts specifically regulated trade with England and Europe, not just intercolonial trade.

options: (A) The laws granted colonial assemblies broad powers to set their own tariffs and regulate trade policy
(B) The laws embodied mercantilist doctrine: colonies existed to enrich the mother country
(C) The laws were repealed within a decade because they lost money
(D) The laws applied only to trade between colonies, not trade with England
items.stem: Beginning in the 1660s, Parliament's Navigation Acts required colonial trade to travel on English ships and pass through English ports. A historian claims these laws show that England viewed the colonies primarily as economic assets to be managed. Which evidence would best support this claim?

stimulus.text: The Navigation Acts (1660s): colonial goods bound for Europe had to ship on English vessels and pass through English ports, enriching English merchants and the crown.

items.explanation: After the Dominion's collapse, Britain was absorbed by European wars and the political settlement of the Glorious Revolution. Loose enforcement was partly a matter of capacity — and in the vacuum, colonial assemblies grew confident and merchants grew rich.
items.fact_source: u2.md §The story — after the Glorious Revolution England briefly tried direct rule through the Dominion of New England (1686-1689), which collapsed; thereafter London mostly practiced 'salutary neglect,' leaving assemblies to grow confident

option_explanations.A: Wrong because Parliament never granted the colonies independence in this era.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the colonies were growing prosperous, not too poor to govern.
option_explanations.C: Right because British preoccupation with European conflicts made sustained colonial oversight impractical.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because no such battles occurred; assemblies grew powerful through neglect, not warfare.

options: (A) Parliament had formally granted the colonies full independence from British imperial rule in 1690
(B) The colonies were too poor to be worth governing
(C) Britain's preoccupation with European wars made sustained colonial oversight impractical
(D) Colonial assemblies had defeated British armies in battle
items.stem: After the collapse of the Dominion of New England in 1689, London largely left the colonies to govern themselves for decades — a practice later called 'salutary neglect.' Which broader development best explains why Britain enforced its colonial laws so loosely?

stimulus.text: The Dominion of New England (1686-1689): James II's attempt to consolidate the northern colonies under one royal governor, which collapsed after the Glorious Revolution.

items.explanation: Tobacco made Virginia viable, and tobacco demanded large numbers of workers. With land abundant (the headright granted 50 acres per migrant financed) and labor scarce, the system produced indentured servants — contracted workers who supplied most of the Chesapeake's workforce before slavery dominated.
items.fact_source: u2.md §The story — the colony survived because of tobacco; the headright system (1618) granted land to anyone financing a migrant's passage, which meant importing indentured servants; §Key terms (Headright system, Indentured servitude)

option_explanations.A: Wrong because England had surplus labor willing to emigrate; the problem was attracting workers to Virginia.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because tobacco was precisely the cash crop that saved the colony.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because in 1618 indentured servants, not enslaved Africans, supplied most Chesapeake labor.
option_explanations.D: Right because the labor-intensive tobacco economy plus abundant land created the demand that indentured servitude filled.

options: (A) England had a shortage of land and sought to keep its workers at home
(B) The Virginia Company refused to grow any cash crop
(C) Enslaved Africans were already cheaper and more available than European servants in 1618
(D) Tobacco demanded large amounts of labor while land was abundant and workers scarce
items.stem: Virginia's headright system (1618) granted land to anyone who paid for a migrant's passage to the colony. Which broader development best explains why this system produced a large population of indentured servants?

stimulus.text: The headright system (1618): 50 acres to anyone paying for a migrant's passage — which meant importing indentured servants for the tobacco fields.

items.explanation: Edwards's revivals told ordinary people they could experience God directly, bypassing established churches. The significance historians stress is political as well as religious: the Awakening split churches into Old and New Lights and taught distrust of established authority — a habit of mind that fed the Revolution.
items.fact_source: u2.md §The story — the First Great Awakening (1730s-1740s) told ordinary people they could experience God directly, splitting churches into Old and New Lights and teaching distrust of established authority

option_explanations.A: Right because the revivals' challenge to church authority carried over into political distrust of authority generally.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the revivals were a colonial religious movement, not a Parliamentary program.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the revivals intensified religious feeling rather than ending it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the Awakening divided churches and drew people away from establishments, not back to the Church of England.

options: (A) The Awakening challenged established churches and taught distrust of traditional authority
(B) The sermons were commissioned by Parliament to keep the colonists obedient to royal authority
(C) They marked the permanent end of all organized religious belief in the colonies
(D) They convinced most colonists to abandon dissenting churches and return to the Church of England
items.stem: 'The bow of God's wrath is bent, and the arrow made ready on the string.' — Jonathan Edwards, 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God,' 1741. Which broader development best explains the historical significance of sermons like this one?

stimulus.text: "The bow of God's wrath is bent, and the arrow made ready on the string, and justice bends the arrow at your heart." — Jonathan Edwards, "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God," Enfield, Connecticut, 1741.

items.explanation: Zenger's acquittal became a landmark for freedom of the press: a colonial printer, tried for criticizing the royal governor, was freed by a jury. It belongs to the broader context of colonists asserting English liberties — alongside Franklin's press culture and the Enlightenment — against royal authority.
items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms (Zenger trial, 1735) — the seditious-libel acquittal of printer John Peter Zenger, a landmark for freedom of the press

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the trial concerned libel and the press, not slavery.
option_explanations.B: Right because the acquittal established a colonial precedent for press freedom against royal power.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the Navigation Acts remained in force long after 1735.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the Great Awakening was a separate religious movement of the 1730s-1740s.

options: (A) It established the legal right of colonists to own enslaved people as property
(B) It became a landmark for press freedom as colonists asserted English liberties
(C) It ended the Navigation Acts
(D) It caused the First Great Awakening by inspiring George Whitefield's preaching tours
items.stem: In 1735, printer John Peter Zenger was acquitted of seditious libel after criticizing New York's royal governor. Which broader development best explains why this trial mattered?

stimulus.text: The Zenger trial (1735): printer John Peter Zenger, tried for seditious libel against New York's royal governor, was acquitted by a jury.

items.explanation: The assembly reflected English political traditions of consent carried across the Atlantic, plus the Virginia Company's practical need: offering political rights helped recruit the settlers the struggling colony desperately needed. Self-government and racial slavery were thus born in the same colony in the same year.
items.fact_source: u2.md §The story — in 1619 two arrivals defined Virginia's future: the House of Burgesses, the first elected assembly in English America, and the first enslaved Africans

option_explanations.A: Wrong because Virginia was a Protestant colony; the pope had no role in its governance.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the assembly grew from English representative traditions, not the Spanish example.
option_explanations.C: Right because English traditions of consent plus the company's need to attract settlers explain the 1619 assembly.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the first enslaved Africans had just arrived in 1619; no such rebellion occurred.

options: (A) A directive from the pope ordering the establishment of Catholic governance in Virginia
(B) The Spanish example of colonial town councils in New Spain and Peru
(C) English consent traditions plus the company's need to attract settlers with rights
(D) A rebellion by enslaved Africans demanding representation in the colonial government
items.stem: Virginia created the House of Burgesses in 1619, the first elected assembly in English America — the same year the first enslaved Africans arrived. Which broader development best explains the creation of the assembly?

stimulus.text: 1619 in Virginia: the House of Burgesses met for the first time — and the first enslaved Africans arrived in the colony.

items.explanation: The historian's reading is supported by sequence: the codes came after Bacon's Rebellion (1676) and amid ongoing conspiracies and uprisings. The review frames slave codes and resistance as cause-and-effect pairs — repression and resistance escalating together — so the laws reveal planters legislating from fear of a system that required constant force.
items.fact_source: u2.md §The story — Virginia's comprehensive slave codes (1705); §What the exam tests here — Stono, the Pueblo Revolt, and slave codes as cause-and-effect pairs: repression and resistance escalating together

option_explanations.A: Wrong because no equivalent English laws governed apprentices as racial property.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the codes defined enslaved status broadly, including the children of enslaved mothers.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because slavery was becoming more, not less, central to the Chesapeake economy.
option_explanations.D: Right because the codes followed decades of uprisings, showing planters using law to contain resistance they feared.

options: (A) The codes were copied directly from English laws governing London apprentices and servants
(B) The codes applied only to newly arrived Africans and exempted those born in Virginia
(C) The codes were passed because slavery was becoming economically unimportant in the Chesapeake
(D) The codes followed decades of resistance, showing slavery required constant legal force
items.stem: Virginia's comprehensive slave codes of 1705 defined enslaved people as property and stripped away legal rights. A historian argues these laws reveal as much about planters' fears as about their power. Which context best supports that interpretation?

stimulus.text: Virginia's slave codes (1705): comprehensive laws defining enslaved people as property, restricting their movement, assembly, and legal rights.

items.explanation: This is the regional comparison the exam stresses most: the Lower South's rice plantations created an exceptionally large demand for enslaved labor, making South Carolina the most slave-dependent colony — the only mainland colony where enslaved people outnumbered free whites.
items.fact_source: u2.md §The story — the Lower South, South Carolina's rice plantations, Georgia (1733), became the most slave-dependent; by the early 1700s enslaved people outnumbered free whites in South Carolina; §What the exam tests here — compare the four regions

option_explanations.A: Right because the rice economy's labor demands produced South Carolina's unique demographic pattern.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because no such freedom-through-conversion policy existed in South Carolina.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because slavery existed in every colonial region, though in different proportions.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because no British law mandated South Carolina's imports; the plantation economy drove them.

options: (A) The Lower South's rice-plantation economy, which created exceptional demand for enslaved labor
(B) South Carolina's policy of granting freedom to enslaved people who converted to Christianity
(C) The complete absence of enslaved people in every other mainland colonial region
(D) A British law requiring South Carolina to import more enslaved workers than all the other colonies
items.stem: By the early 1700s, enslaved people outnumbered free whites in South Carolina — a demographic pattern found nowhere else in the mainland colonies. Which broader development best explains this pattern?

stimulus.text: South Carolina's rice plantations made the Lower South the most slave-dependent region; by the early 1700s, enslaved people outnumbered free whites there.
